Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Arjun Patel, a 36-year-old South Asian detective, came to treatment after years of carrying a childhood history that had never felt fully in the past. He grew up in a home where a caregiver’s physical abuse was unpredictable and humiliating, and even now he spoke of that period as something that had shaped the way he moved through the world without ever fully leaving it behind. As a boy, he had learned to read the sound of a door opening or slamming as if it were a warning, because in his mind that noise could mean someone was about to enter with anger. He also remembered the shock of certain temperatures on his skin — a cold draft, the abrupt chill of a room, even the feel of cool air after a shower — because those sensations seemed to pull him back into the helplessness of being a child who could not control what happened to him. The most unsettling moments were often at night, especially when he was alone in bed or staying in an unfamiliar place, when the quiet of the room made him feel exposed and on edge in a way he could not easily dismiss.

By adulthood, Arjun had built a life that looked orderly from the outside. He married, kept a demanding job as a detective, and was known as someone reliable under pressure. Yet over time he began arranging his days around the kinds of situations he dreaded. He avoided people when he could, skipping informal gatherings, keeping conversations brief, and finding reasons not to linger in shared spaces. He also delayed sleep night after night, staying up very late so that he would not have to face the feeling of being alone in the dark or the vulnerability of lying awake in a room by himself. When work allowed, he avoided going out unless it was absolutely necessary, preferring to remain in controlled environments where he could anticipate who was around him and what noises might startle him. These habits gradually narrowed his world in practical ways. He became more isolated from others, and his wife began to notice how often he declined plans or insisted on staying home after work. At his job, he managed to perform, but he found himself carefully positioning himself in relation to exits and listening for doors in a way that felt automatic and draining.

Arjun described the present as a life in which he was constantly bracing for something that others did not seem to notice. A door slamming in the station or in his home could make his body tighten before he had time to think. Sleeping alone, whether because his wife was away or because he was in an unfamiliar place on a case, left him restless and watchful, unable to settle in the way he wished he could. Even a shift in temperature against his skin could jolt him into a brief, vivid sense of unease, as if his body recognized danger before his mind could name it. These moments did not come with a simple explanation that satisfied him; instead, they fed a painful inner story that had become increasingly difficult to ignore. Arjun had come to believe that the way he reacted after what happened showed that he was a lousy coper, someone whose responses were somehow inadequate despite years of forcing himself to function. He spoke with visible strain about feeling as though he did not know himself anymore, as if the man he had become was unfamiliar even to him. More troubling still was the sense that there was something wrong with him as a person, a belief that settled in whenever he noticed himself backing away from others or needing to control his surroundings so carefully.

Although he continued working, Arjun’s confidence in his own steadiness had worn thin. He could manage investigations and take charge in the field, yet he was haunted by the contrast between the composed detective others saw and the private fear he carried into ordinary moments at home. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing realization that he could no longer explain away the strain on his marriage, his social life, and his sense of self. He wanted relief from the constant vigilance around doors, temperature changes, and sleeping alone, but just as strongly, he wanted to know whether he was truly as broken as he feared. In asking for help, he was hoping not only to sleep without delaying the night for as long as possible, but also to discover whether there was any way to feel like himself again.
